facts.text: Breeding adults have an unstreaked orange breast bordered with dark markings below, plus a white V on the back.
facts.quote: The breeding adult has an unstreaked orange breast, bordered with dark markings below, and a white V on its back.

facts.text: Red-necked stints are highly gregarious, forming flocks with other small waders such as sharp-tailed sandpipers and curlew sandpipers.
facts.quote: Red-necked stints are highly gregarious and will form flocks with other small Calidris waders, such as sharp-tailed sandpipers and curlew sandpipers in their non-breeding areas.

facts.text: Both parents incubate the clutch of 3 or 4 eggs for 20–22 days, but the female leaves soon after hatching.
facts.quote: The clutch of 3 or 4 eggs is incubated for 20-22 days by both parents. The females leaves soon after the eggs hatch while the male continues to care for the chicks until they fledge at 16-17 days.

facts.text: Red-necked stints spend the non-breeding season in Southeast Asia and Australasia, as far south as Tasmania and New Zealand.
facts.quote: Red-necked stints are strongly migratory, breeding along the Arctic littoral of eastern Eurasia and spending the non-breeding season in Southeast Asia and Australasia as far south as Tasmania and New Zealand.

facts.text: The species was formally described in 1776 by the German naturalist Peter Simon Pallas.
facts.quote: The red-necked stint was formally described in 1776 by the German naturalist Peter Simon Pallas under the binomial name Trynga ruficollis.

facts.text: Its scientific name ruficollis is Modern Latin for "red-necked".
facts.quote: The specific epithet ruficollis is Modern Latin meaning "red-necked" from Latin rufus meaning "red" or "rufous" and -collis meaning "-necked" or "-throated".

facts.text: It breeds on low altitude tundra, usually in dry raised areas, and lays its eggs in June.
facts.quote: The breeding habitat is low altitude tundra usually in dry raised areas. The birds have only a low degree of site fidelity. The eggs are laid in June.

facts.text: The male cares for the chicks until they fledge at 16-17 days, and only a single brood is raised each year.
facts.quote: the male continues to care for the chicks until they fledge at 16-17 days. Only a single brood is raised each year.

facts.text: It forages in wet grassland and soft mud, mainly picking up food by sight.
facts.quote: They forage in wet grassland and soft mud, mainly picking up food by sight.

facts.text: In its non-breeding habitat it feeds on intertidal mudflats and along the muddy margins of freshwater lakes.
facts.quote: In their non-breeding habitat they feed on intertidal mudflats and along the muddy margins of freshwater lakes.
